Fit
fit
adj. (suitable, qualified, proper for a purpose)
Of uncertain origin, meaning apt or suited. The Authorized Version uses it for men fit for war, a man fit to lead the scapegoat away, conduct fit in the Lord, and the solemn negative — not fit for the kingdom of God.

Biblical Definition

The most searching use is our Lord's: “No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luk 9:62). The image is exact — a ploughman who turns his head cuts a crooked furrow — and it was said to a man whose request was entirely reasonable: let me first go bid them farewell at home. Divided attention, not open rebellion, is what unfits him. On the Day of Atonement the live goat was sent away “by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness” (Lev 16:21), bearing all the iniquities of Israel upon his head into a land not inhabited. The Hebrew margin reads a man of opportunity, a man ready and appointed for it. Chronicles uses the word of David's Gadites, “men of war fit for the battle, that could handle shield and buckler, whose faces were like the faces of lions” (1Ch 12:8). Proverbs applies it to the order of a young man's life: “Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house” (Pro 24:27) — field before house, provision before establishment. And Paul uses it of the creational order in the home: “Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord” (Col 3:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fit as suitable, convenient, meet, becoming; and qualified, competent, prepared for a purpose.

expand to see more

FIT, a. Suitable; convenient; meet; becoming.

1. Qualified; as, a man is fit for an office.

2. Prepared; ready.

FIT, v.t. To adapt; to suit; to make suitable.

FITNESS, n. Suitableness; adaptedness; propriety.

Key Scripture

Luk 9:62 — "And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."

Lev 16:21 — "And Aaron shall lay both his hands upon the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities of the children of Israel, and all their transgressions in all their sins, putting them upon the head of the goat, and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness:"

Col 3:18 — "Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as it is fit in the Lord."

Pro 24:27 — "Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house."

Modern Corruption

“As it is fit in the Lord” is treated as a cultural leftover; Paul grounds the household order in creation, not in custom.

expand to see more

Colossians 3:18 is regularly explained away as first-century household convention that the gospel has since dissolved. The explanation cannot survive the way the apostles actually argue. Paul grounds headship in the creation order, not in Roman custom — for Adam was first formed, then Eve (1Ti 2:13) — and in the relation of Christ to the church (Eph 5:22-33), which is not a cultural arrangement. Peter appeals to Sarah, centuries before any Greco-Roman code (1Pe 3:5-6). And the same passages bind the husband to a love measured by Christ's giving of Himself, which no surrounding culture had ever required. What Scripture calls fit in the Lord is an ordered mutual self-giving, and it is neither the tyranny it is caricatured as nor the interchangeability offered in its place.

The second thing to hold is Luke 9:62, which is the sharpest word in the entry. The man who was refused had asked to say goodbye to his family. Nothing in the request was wicked; it simply revealed a divided heart at the moment of call. A ploughman looking back leaves a crooked furrow, and the kingdom is not served by men whose attention is behind them. This is not a doctrine of sinless devotion — Peter looked back, wept, and was restored — but it is a refusal to enlist anyone on the understanding that Christ may have what is left over.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'itti (H6261), timely, ready, appointed — the fit man of Leviticus 16; 'arak (H6186), to set in order; Greek euthetos (G2111), well-placed, fit for use.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'itti (H6261) — timely, ready, appointed for the occasion; Leviticus 16:21, the fit man who led away the scapegoat — its only occurrence.

Hebrew 'azazel (H5799) — the scapegoat, the goat of departure; the live goat that bore the iniquities away.

Greek euthetos (G2111) — well-placed, useful, fit; Luke 9:62, 14:35, Hebrews 6:7.

Greek aroton / arotron (G723) — a plough; Luke 9:62, the only New Testament occurrence.

Greek aneko (G433) — to be proper, becoming, fitting; Colossians 3:18, Ephesians 5:4, Philemon 8.

Usage

"“Having put his hand to the plough, and looking back” — a crooked furrow."

"“By the hand of a fit man into the wilderness” — a man appointed for it."

"“Prepare thy work without… and afterwards build thine house”."
